title: Spatial Experiences
summary: Sanitized view of marker-based AR, model viewers, WebXR entry points, and WebGL laboratories used to prove athletic and brand stories in space—not only on a flat page.
role: Creative technologist and software engineer — scene architecture, capability gates, interaction hints, and packaging for event deployments
timeframe: Nike Digital Athlete / SME experiences and ongoing portfolio laboratories, 2021–2026
problem: Event and brand teams need enough spatial fidelity for people to feel a product or venue story, while devices, browsers, cameras, and networks fail in uneven ways that a flat marketing page never has to explain.
constraints: Employer, athlete, and campaign-specific assets remain abstracted or removed.
WebXR, camera permissions, and model formats differ across iOS Quick Look, Android Scene Viewer, desktop WebGL, and headset paths.
Marker tracking and large GLTF/GLB payloads must degrade into a useful 2D path instead of a blank canvas.
Packaging for Men's World Cup, World Athletics Championships, and playground builds had to stay reproducible without treating any single demo as the only truth.
approach: Start from the decision the scene must unlock: try-on feel, venue presence, or geometric literacy—not from a library preference.
Separate capability detection (WebXR session, camera, and model-viewer modes) from the scene graph so unsupported devices get an honest next action.
Prototype with Three.js and Babylon.js where real-time interaction matters; use Google model-viewer for Quick Look, Scene Viewer, and WebXR packaging when distribution beats custom engine work.
Ship marker-based AR (AR.js, Three.js, and GLTF) with QR entry, UI hints, and troubleshooting affordances as first-class product surfaces.
Keep a personal WebGL laboratory—tesseract wireframes, orbit controls, and helix motion—so spatial intuition stays inspectable outside any client repository.
